conservation.notes: Endemic to New Zealand and protected since the Wildlife Act 1953. Numbers were numerous until the 1960s but have since declined through introduced predators (possums, rats, cats, stoats), hunting and habitat degradation. Whether kererū are present at a site now depends on forest cover, forest type and predator density.

human_tolerance.notes: Found in native lowland forest, scrub, the countryside and city gardens and parks, from coastal to montane. Settles in parks and large gardens when fruiting trees are present, but flushes early and often, and is a common road casualty.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Breeding depends on the availability of ripe fruit, which varies seasonally, annually and by location. Further south it runs from October (early spring) to April (late summer/early autumn); in the warmer Northland region kererū can raise young year-round given enough fruit. The southern end of the sourced October-April window is trimmed here so this phase does not overlap the sourced March-May moult, which the source says suppresses breeding. The male performs steep display flights, ascending and appearing to stall at the top before a swooping descent.

phases.name: moult
phases.note: Kererū do not breed when moulting, which tends to take place between March and May.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: Authored judgement: outside the breeding and moult windows kererū are sedentary and hold foraging territories in fruiting trees, dispersing locally to follow fruit. Fieldwork showed most birds moving up to 25 km within their range looking for food, with longer movements recorded.

vocalizations.description: An occasional soft coo. The wings also make a characteristic loud whoosh in flight, and the flight itself is distinctive, with birds often ascending slowly before steep parabolic dives.

external.note: iNaturalist (P3151), NCBI (P685) and eBird (P3444) ids via Wikidata; GBIF usage key 2495905 matches the GBIF backbone and the ITIS TSN comes from Wikidata P815.

common_names.note: English, French, German and Dutch names from Wikidata P1843. English follows the IOC World Bird List designation 'New Zealand pigeon'; 'kererū' and 'kūkupa' are the Māori names recorded on the same Wikidata property and in the article's Common names section.

range.note: Endemic to New Zealand, found from Northland to Stewart Island and offshore islands; the extinct Norfolk Island subspecies aside, the article names no other native landmass, and Wikidata P183 records New Zealand as the country it is endemic to.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Powered flight with slow ascent and steep parabolic dives is described in the Description section; walking is the ground gait a frugivorous pigeon uses between trees, and the shared program needs a ground gait for foraging. AVONET classifies the species as a forest, fruit-eating, insessorial pigeon.

traits.nest_type.note: 'Both birds construct the unlined platform of twigs - mostly kanuka ... which can be up to 30 cm across', in the canopy of trees, bushes, shrubs or hedges 1.8-9.1 m above the ground.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg: 0.653 kg falls in the Small band (Small is anything under 1 kg in this schema).

traits.mass_kg.note: AVONET Mass = 653 g (mean of 8 individuals, Mass.Source Dunning), consistent with Wikipedia's 550-850 g.

traits.length_m.note: Wikipedia gives only an upper figure, 'up to 50 cm in length', which is used directly; a typical bird is somewhat shorter, so this is an upper bound rather than a mean.

traits.wingspan_m.note: Wikipedia: 'a wingspan of around 75 cm'. Wikidata Q1145127 P2050 independently records 75 cm.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Midpoint of 'Kererū have a lifespan of 15 to 25 years'; the same section records a 29-year-old bird recaptured in Rotorua in 2020 after 24 years.

traits.diet.note: Wikipedia's Feeding section: 'primarily frugivorous, preferring fruit from native trees, but also eating leaves, flowers and buds' and 'fruit comprises the major part of its diet, the kererū also browses on leaves and buds ... especially nitrogen-rich foliage during breeding'. AVONET independently classifies it as Trophic.Level Herbivore, Trophic.Niche Frugivore. Shares derive from that statement: fruit 0.65, browse 0.35.

traits.social.note: 'The kererū is monogamous; pairs are thought to reproduce together over multiple seasons, and remain together when not breeding', with both birds building the nest and both incubating in shifts of around six hours. group_size 1-4 in a pair's own terms; the upper bound of 6 allows small feeding aggregations at a good fruit tree.

traits.defense.note: Authored from the sourced account of aggressive male display flights and territorial disputes over fruiting trees: a kererū's answer to a rival or a threat is to fly up and away, so Flee rather than Mob. The display flight is a courtship and territorial signal, not a defence against a predator.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: 0.4. Kererū settle in city gardens and parks and habituate to people, but they are large, ground-striding birds that flush early and often, and the article notes kererū as frequent roadkill.

habitat.use.note: Wikipedia calls it 'a large arboreal pigeon' and AVONET Habitat = Forest with Primary.Lifestyle = Insessorial; foraging is in the canopy, with some ground feeding. arboreal 0.85 / ground 0.15.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Authored: the nest is built in 'the canopy of trees, bushes, shrubs, or hedges', so shrub_thicket is the closest available shelter tag.

habitat.resources.note: Feeding section for fruit (native trees, especially Lauraceae and Arecaceae, podocarps such as miro and kahikatea, and introduced elder, privet and plums), leaves, buds and flowers; Breeding and lifespan for the twig platform and the canopy nest; the bird 'displays typical pigeon behaviour, including drinking by suction', which is why water is a resource. Monthly weighting of the browse share was left out because the article says leaves can comprise most of the diet at certain times of the year but does not date that.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Environment and distribution section: the kererū is found in 'native lowland forest, scrub, the countryside, and city gardens and parks', so Adapter is the matching affinity rather than Exploiter. road_mortality High follows from the article's discussion of kererū as a common roadkill; light_max and flight_distance_m are authored judgements.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'Although sedentary, kererū can move considerable distances within their range' and AVONET Migration = 1 (sedentary): a resident that moves locally to track fruit, so ActiveYearRound.

seasonal.phases.note: Breeding section: fruit-dependent breeding, the October-April window in the south, year-round breeding possible in the warm north, the March-May moult that suppresses breeding, the male's steep display flight, and local movements of up to 25 km (and up to 100 km for some Southland birds) tracking fruit. The end of the territorial phase is an authored judgement, and the breeding phase is restricted to NZ-AUK so a South Island population reads differently.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Breeding section: a single oval white egg of 49 x 34 mm, incubated 28-29 days by both parents, and a chick that fledges after 30-45 days. duration_days is the midpoint of each sourced range (28.5 for the egg, 37.5 for the nestling to fledging).

vocalizations.coo.note: Description section: 'Kererū make occasional soft coo sounds, and their wings make a characteristic "whoosh" during flight.' The coo is the only true vocalisation the cited source describes; the wing whoosh is included in the same description as flight noise rather than claimed as a separate call, because the source does not call it one.

look.note: Description section for the plumage: dark green head, neck and upper breast with gold-bronze highlights; copper-sheened purple nape, upper back and secondary coverts; grey-green lower back, rump and rest of upper wing; dark brown tail with green highlights; sharply demarcated white breast; pale grey undertail and underwing coverts; red bill with an orange tip, dark red feet and red eyes with a pink orbital ring; juveniles paler with duller bill, eye and feet and a shorter tail. Proportions are authored from AVONET's measurements for this species (culmen 29.6 mm, tarsus 34.5 mm, wing 256.6 mm, Kipps distance 81.4 mm, tail 193.2 mm) read against the biped_winged body plan: a relatively small head on a long body, short legs, a long square tail, and a broad, moderately long wing. wing_aspect is anchored on the sourced 75 cm span over the 256.6 mm chord (half-span/chord about 1.46, rounded to 1.5).

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program, which is a rough fit for a large frugivorous pigeon and is the least-bad of the four shared programs: its ground-foraging, perching and alarm structure suits a canopy pigeon better than the mammal, anuran or seabird programs do. food_tag is fruit because fruit is the major part of the diet. Both song and alarm point at the single sourced call, coo, because the cited source describes no other vocalisation. nest_m1/nest_m2 are 10 and 2 for the sourced October-April breeding window; the shared program wraps that around its own hard-coded spring months, so nest-building renders in October-February rather than across the full October-April span. flee_m 18 and song_cooldown_s 25 are judgements for a large, flighty, soft-voiced bird.
